questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of low-grade fever, cough, and wheezing. He was known to have COPD. His chest X-ray showed no infiltrates. He was sent home with prescriptions for azithromycin and prednisone for treatment of presumed COPD exacerbation. Two days later, his blood cultures returned positive.
questions.lead_in: What organism should prompt urgent re-evaluation?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus S. aureus is an aggressive pathogen that can cause a variety of potentially life-threatening syndromes. When recovered Induration of ≥5 mm Induration of ≥10 mm Induration of ≥15 mm HIV infected persons Recent immigrants (less than 5 years) from high-prevalence countries Considered positive in any person Recent contact of a person with TB Injection drug users Persons with fibrotic changes on chest radiograph consistent with prior TB Residents and employees of high-risk congregate settings Patients with organ transplants Mycobacteriology laboratory personnel Persons who are immunosuppressed for other reasons Children less than 4 years Persons with clinical conditions that place them at high risk Infants, children, and adolescents exposed to adults in high-risk categories from blood cultures, it should not be regarded as a contaminant. Patients with blood cultures that are positive for S. aureus require thorough evaluation for sites of infection, exclusion of infective endocarditis, and parenteral IV antibiotic therapy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q14

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of dyspnea and a nonproductive cough. Four weeks earlier he had returned from a holiday in West Africa where he had bought components for drums, which he then crafted himself. He had a history of hypertension, obesity, and type 2 diabetes. On examination, he appeared ill. His blood pressure was 85/46mmHg, heart rate was 115 beats/minute, respiratory rate was 32 breaths/minute, and oxygen saturations were 86% on 4LPM oxygen. He required urgent intubation and transfer to the critical care unit. Investigations: CXR: small bilateral effusions seen with cardiomegaly 4 sets of blood cultures positive at 12 hours with grampositive rods
questions.lead_in: What infection prevention intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Doxycycline prophylaxis for healthcare workers exposed to droplets
Immunization for all healthcare worker providing direct care

questions.explanation: Standard precautions only These materials used as drum heads can be contaminated with anthrax spores. The patient is not at risk to those around him and therefore requires only standard precautions. The exposure does need to be pursued, and there may be family and friends that require chemoprophylaxis. The healthcare workers that came into contact with him do not need immunization or chemoprophylaxis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q42

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man in Kyrgyzstan presented with painless lesions on both arms. The lesions had begun as pruritic papules but had then enlarged, becoming vesicular, coalescing into bullae and developing significant local and spreading edema. He had systemic symptoms of chills and fever. The patient worked on a farm and had handled cattle 6 days earlier. On examination there was extensive edema and hemorrhagic bullae in both arms. He had tender lymphadenopathy in both axillae. His temperature was 37.9°C. Swabs were taken of the vesicular fluid, and a full-thickness punch biopsy was taken. Blood cultures were also sent. Microscopy using polychrome methylene blue stain showed blue-colored bacilli with light pink-colored capsules.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate antimicrobial?
questions.explanation: Benzylpenicillin Penicillin is the drug of choice in naturally occurring anthrax. This can either be oral or intramuscular in mild uncomplicated cutaneous anthrax or intravenous in complicated or severe cutaneous anthrax. Penicillin is used in combination with other antimicrobials such as clindamycin and ciprofloxacin in inhalational anthrax or with streptomycin in gastrointestinal infection. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q41

questions.stem: There was a reported bioterrorist release of anthrax spores in a crowd at a professional football game in an outdoor stadium. The announcement about the release of the spores was made 3 hours after the game ended. Rapid testing confirmed contamination at the stadium with anthrax spores, and PCR confirmed Bacillus anthracis.
questions.lead_in: What would be the most appropriate immediate management of those who attended the game?

options.text: Anthrax immune globulin and 3 doses of anthrax vaccine
Hospitalization with respiratory isolation for those in contaminated seats
Self-taken nasal swab to determine whether exposed

questions.explanation: Prophylaxis with ciprofloxacin or doxycycline Nasal swabs are not indicated in this setting as everyone at the stadium would be presumed to have been exposed. Although ciprofloxacin and doxycycline are contraindicated in pregnancy and in children, they are both recommended as prophylaxis for anthrax exposure. If sensitivities of B. anthracis return as penicillin-susceptible, the regimen can then be changed to amoxicillin. Hospitalization is not required unless symptomatic. Anthrax immune globulin is indicated for the treatment of inhalational anthrax. Anthrax vaccine may be indicated for exposure in a mass-incident exposure such as this, but not in combination with immune globulin.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q26

questions.question: A woman travels to Tanzania and climbs Mount Kilimanjaro. She presents with a fever and eschar.

cohort_answer.text: African trypanosomiasis; Tularemia; Rickettsia africae (African tick bite fever); Scrub typhus; Bacillus anthracis; Plague.

questions.question: There is a patient with "hemorrhagic bullous lesions" in a peripheral hospital. It has been transported to your laboratory: non-motile, non-hemolytic. Gram stain shows large GPB.

parts.text: What 2 things should you do right away?
What 3 tests would you use to identify the organism?
You wish to send this specimen off to the reference laboratory. What are 3 issues you need to do when transporting specimens?

questions.model_answer: a) Two immediate actions: (1) Notify infection prevention and control/public health and the laboratory director immediately (possible Bacillus anthracis, a Tier 1 select agent/bioterrorism concern). (2) Handle the specimen within a biosafety cabinet using BSL-2/3 precautions, halt further routine bench workup, and refer to a reference/public health laboratory (Laboratory Response Network) for confirmatory testing. b) Three tests to identify the organism: (1) Lysis by gamma phage (specific for B. anthracis). (2) Direct fluorescent antibody testing for the capsule (poly-D-glutamic acid) and cell wall antigens. (3) PCR for B. anthracis-specific virulence genes (toxin genes on pXO1, capsule gene on pXO2). c) Three issues when transporting the specimen to reference lab: (1) Proper triple packaging per Category A infectious substance shipping regulations (UN2814). (2) Complete chain-of-custody documentation. (3) Advance notification of the receiving reference laboratory and appropriate biosafety labeling/transport by an approved carrier.
questions.beyond_mandell: CDC Laboratory Response Network/select agent shipping regulations

parts.text: Name 1 rickettsial, 1 bacterial (non-rickettsia) and 1 viral cause of eschar and the clinical syndrome that it causes.

questions.model_answer: Rickettsial: Rickettsia africae - African tick-bite fever (eschar, often multiple, with fever and regional lymphadenopathy). Bacterial (non-rickettsial): Bacillus anthracis - cutaneous anthrax (painless necrotic eschar with surrounding edema). Viral: an orthopoxvirus (e.g., mpox virus) - mpox, whose skin lesions can crust into an eschar-like scab.

questions.question: Blood culture is positive for Bacillus.

parts.text: How to tell if anthracis and results from tests?
What is another major bacillus species implicated in human disease?

cohort_answer.text: B. anthracis: (non)Motility, (non)hemolysis, Gamma phage testing or PCR, and pen S. Non motile, spore forming, non hemolysis. Other bacillus involved in human diseases: B. cereus: gastroenteritis, bacteremia. B. subtilis = rare cause of pneumonia, bacteremia, septicemia (usually in patients with hematologic malignancy or some other severe immune compromise) and may cause foodborne disease (diarrheal illness similar to B. cereus). B. licheniformis = associated with outbreak of bacteremia in immunocompromised due to contaminated cotton wool, and a well-established cause of central-line infections. All other species are motiles or +/- motil. R to pen except B. cereus biovar anthracis.

parts.text: A) What lab test do you do to distinguish it from non-anthracis strains?

cohort_answer.text: Lysis of gamma-phage; Detection of PGA capsule by fluorescent antibody; Identify toxin genes by PCR; MALDI-TOF. [Background: B. anthracis is nonhemolytic on sheep/horse blood agar and nonmotile, whereas most other clinical isolates are motile and beta-hemolytic]

parts.text: B) What does the gram stain look like?

cohort_answer.text: Large encapsulated gram positive bacilli; Long chains with central oval spores (clearing); Aerobic; Non-hemolytic; Spore-forming; Colonies look like "Medusa's head" aka "comet tail" referring to slightly curled periphery

parts.text: C) What other non-anthracis strain is seen frequently?

Government official opens envelope, white powder released. Letter says it is anthrax spores.

parts.text: What 3 immediate public health measures would you take?

cohort_answer.text: Contact Public Health; Notify lab on suspicion of anthrax to confirm dx; Contact tracing; Post-exposure ppx; Decontaminate all contacts thoroughly

questions.question:
Q27 (2003 PM)
Government official opens envelope, white powder released. Letter says it is anthrax spores.

parts.text: B) What ppx would you recommend to a patient exposed to anthrax spores?

cohort_answer.text: Cipro 500mg PO BID or Doxy 100mg PO BID x 60 days. Alternatives: Levofloxacin, Moxifloxacin, Clindamycin. If PCN susceptible: Amox 1g PO TID or Pen VK 500mg PO q6h. Vaccine 3 doses at 0, 2, 4 weeks

questions.question:
Q27 (2003 PM)
Government official opens envelope, white powder released. Letter says it is anthrax spores.

parts.text: C) 3 sites of infection and mechanism of how those infections occur

cohort_answer.text: Cutaneous anthrax – contact with contaminated animal source with trivial skin trauma (wool, hair, bone, meat, horns, hides), or injection of heroin contaminated with spores. Inhalational anthrax – inhalation of spores. Gastrointestinal anthrax – ingesting undercooked meat from infected animal

questions.question: Q4 (2003 PM). Necrotizing pneumonia. Farmer on prednisone, cleans barns; develops necrotizing pneumonia. Gram stain of blood shows GPB.

cohort_answer.text: Rhodococcus equi. Clinical: mainly affects immunocompromised hosts (recognized opportunistic infection in HIV); pulmonary infections most common (cavitary lesions, lung consolidation, indistinguishable from TB). Micro: pleomorphic GPR (coccoid to bacillary), early colonies small/white (resembling diphtheroids, contaminant risk), salmon-pink colonies appear days 4-7, sometimes stains acid fast (confused with mycobacteria). Epi: found in soil worldwide, thrives in marine/freshwater habitats, infects land/water animals; human acquisition via inhalation, wound/mucous membrane inoculation, or ingestion from exposure to domesticated animals (horses, pigs). Treatment: coryneform bacteria uniformly susceptible to glycopeptides (vancomycin, teicoplanin), most susceptible to daptomycin/linezolid; R. equi usually susceptible to vancomycin, teicoplanin, erythromycin, FQ, rifampin, carbapenems, aminoglycosides, linezolid; macrolide + rifampin combination most commonly used for minimum 2 months in immunocompromised host.

parts.text: List 1 infection (causative organism not required) under each category that cause an eschar - Rickettsial

cohort_answer.text: Rickettsial: Scrub typhus, murine typhus, epidemic typhus, african tick bite fever (Orientia tsutsugamushi, rickettsia africae). Bacterial (non-rickettsial): Tularemia, plague (Francisella tularensis, yersinia pestis); Ecthyma (pseudomonas). Virus: Smallpox, vaccinia
